items.prompt: An editor has completed edits `type A`, then `type B`, and stores completed edits in a stack. The user now issues one Undo command. Which pop rule is correct?
constraints: Use the exact output, strictness, scan direction, and tie semantics stated in the prompt.
Do not classify the algorithm from a variable name or one intermediate snapshot.

options.text: Pop `type B`: Undo explicitly reverses the most recently completed edit, regardless of either edit’s payload.
Compare the text inserted by A and B, then pop whichever edit has the larger payload.
Pop both edits because reaching an empty stack is the invariant of every stack operation.
Push the Undo command as an edit, then pop it; this reverses `type B` indirectly.

feedback.reason: Undo’s contract selects the latest completed edit, so the LIFO top `type B` is removed without a value-order comparison.

blocks.text: A normal LIFO stack removes an entry because an operation requests the most recent pending or completed item. After A then B, the top is B, so one Undo pops and reverses B; A remains available for a later Undo. No ordering relation between the edit payloads is relevant. Comparing payload sizes invents a requirement, emptying the stack undoes too much, and pushing then popping the Undo command leaves B untouched. Reusable rule: derive an ordinary stack pop from a semantic event such as undo, close, return, or finish—not from the mere presence of values that could be compared.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.target_false_heuristic: Undo is defined by completion order, not by the size or lexical order of an edit’s payload; this comparison can select A even though B is the latest edit.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.surface_feature_classifier: One Undo reverses one latest edit. Emptying the stack would also reverse A and therefore changes the requested result.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.unjustified_alternative_rule: Popping the newly pushed Undo command only removes that command; the completed edit B remains on top and is not reversed.

items.prompt: While validating `([x])`, the stack of unmatched openers is `(` below `[`, and the current token is `]`. Which rule correctly handles this closer?
constraints: Use the exact output, strictness, scan direction, and tie semantics stated in the prompt.
Do not classify the algorithm from a variable name or one intermediate snapshot.

options.text: Compare delimiter character codes and pop every opener smaller than `]`.
Pop both `[` and `(` because every closer ends all currently open structures.
Push `]` first and postpone matching until the end of the input.
Verify that `]` matches the top `[`, then pop exactly `[`, leaving `(` pending.

feedback.reason: Proper nesting requires the closer to match and remove exactly the most recent unmatched opener, the left-square-bracket token.

blocks.text: Each retained entry is an unmatched opener. Proper nesting says that a closer must match the newest such opener, so `]` is checked against the top `[`, then `[` alone is popped; the older `(` remains for the later `)`. Character-code ordering has no nesting meaning, popping both openers would close `(` with the wrong token, and postponing all checks can retain an already-invalid prefix. Reusable rule: delimiter-stack removal is controlled by type match plus LIFO nesting, not numeric dominance.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.target_false_heuristic: Delimiter character codes do not encode which opener is structurally pending; the only legal candidate is the LIFO top of the matching type.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.surface_feature_classifier: The current `]` closes `[`, not the older `(`. Popping both would accept an invalid nesting transition.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.unjustified_alternative_rule: A closer is not a new pending opener. Deferring the check loses the opportunity to reject the first mismatched prefix immediately.

items.prompt: The postfix stack contains values for the expression `8 3 -`. Order the transition for the `-` operator.
constraints: Order the steps by semantic dependency, not by the order in which they are listed.
The canonical scoring contract awards preserved adjacent relations.

elements.text: Push the result 5 as one completed subresult.
Pop 3 as the right operand.
Pop 8 as the left operand.
Compute 8 - 3.

feedback.reason: Binary postfix evaluation must pop the right operand before the left, apply `left - right`, and push the one resulting subexpression.

items: Pop the top `3`; because `-` is binary postfix, this most recent subresult is the right operand.
Pop the next value `8` as the left operand.
Apply the operator in preserved order: `8 - 3 = 5`, not `3 - 8`.
Push `5`, which now represents the complete subexpression.

blocks.text: This is an ordinary operand stack: arity and operand position trigger its pops. Reordering the pops changes non-commutative operators, applying before both operands are available is undefined, and pushing before evaluation would place an uncomputed value on the stack. Reusable rule: for a binary postfix operator, first pop right, then left, compute `left op right`, then push the result.

items.prompt: Scan temperatures left to right and, for every day, return the nearest later day with a strictly warmer temperature; equal temperatures do not qualify. When the current temperature is `75` and the unresolved stack top is `73`, which rule is correct?
constraints: Use the exact output, strictness, scan direction, and tie semantics stated in the prompt.
Do not classify the algorithm from a variable name or one intermediate snapshot.

options.text: Push the current entry before checking the top, then repair any broken state afterward without changing the resulting answers.
Pop while current value is strictly greater than the top candidate value.
Pop on greater-or-equal even when equal is not a valid answer.
Pop until the stack is empty; the stopping relation and answer timing are implementation details that cannot affect correctness.

feedback.reason: Because the current day is the first later day strictly warmer than each smaller unresolved top, pop while `current > top` and finalize those days.

blocks.text: A retained index is a day whose nearest strictly warmer day has not appeared. At current `75`, every smaller value on the top suffix is resolved: this is the first qualifying day encountered to its right, so pop its index and write the distance. Stop at a top `>= 75`; an equal `75` is not warmer, and a larger top is not resolved. Popping on `>=` would falsely answer equal-temperature days, popping to empty would discard unresolved hotter days, and pushing current first would hide the candidates it should resolve. Reusable rule: for next strictly greater in a left-to-right scan, resolve exactly the top suffix satisfying `stackValue < current`.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.target_false_heuristic: With a strictly-warmer contract, equal temperature is not a valid answer; `>=` would finalize a day at an unqualified equal value.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.surface_feature_classifier: A top at `80` remains unresolved when current is `75`; emptying the stack would discard a candidate without finding its warmer day.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.unjustified_alternative_rule: Pushing `75` first makes it the top and blocks access to smaller unresolved days that `75` should resolve.

items.prompt: Scan latencies left to right and return, for each position, the nearest later latency that is strictly smaller; equal values do not qualify. When current latency is `4` and the unresolved top is `5`, which pop rule follows?
constraints: Use the exact output, strictness, scan direction, and tie semantics stated in the prompt.
Do not classify the algorithm from a variable name or one intermediate snapshot.

options.text: Pop while current value is strictly smaller than the top candidate value.
A decreasing stack is always used regardless of requested relation.
Pop until the stack is empty; the stopping relation and answer timing are implementation details that cannot affect correctness.
Push the current entry before checking the top, then repair any broken state afterward without changing the resulting answers.

feedback.reason: Current `4` is the first later strictly smaller value for every larger top candidate, so pop exactly while `current < top`.

blocks.text: Each retained index still lacks a strictly smaller value to its right. The current `4` qualifies for top `5`, and scan order proves it is the nearest qualifying value, so `5` is popped and finalized. Continue only while the top is greater than `4`; stop at `<= 4`, because equality is not smaller and a lower top is unresolved. A fixed “decreasing stack” slogan cannot derive this direction, popping to empty loses valid candidates, and pushing current first hides the suffix that current resolves. Reusable rule: translate the requested relation directly—next strictly smaller uses `current < stackTop` in a left-to-right resolving scan.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.target_false_heuristic: The maintained direction depends on the requested next-smaller relation; a memorized decreasing-stack rule would use the wrong comparison here.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.surface_feature_classifier: A top at `3` has not found a smaller answer when current is `4`; popping it merely to empty storage destroys unresolved state.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.unjustified_alternative_rule: After pushing `4`, the new top prevents `4` from resolving the older `5`; the required transition must process the old frontier first.

items.prompt: Scan left to right and return each position’s nearest previous index with a strictly greater value; equals do not qualify. Order the operations for one current value.
constraints: Order the steps by semantic dependency, not by the order in which they are listed.
The canonical scoring contract awards preserved adjacent relations.

elements.text: Write the current position’s previous-greater result.
Push the current value and its index as a candidate for later positions.
Pop top candidates that are not greater than the current value under the declared strictness.
Read the surviving top as the previous greater candidate, or record no answer if the stack is empty.

feedback.reason: For a previous-strictly-greater query, remove non-greater candidates, read the nearest surviving left index, write it, and only then push current.

items: Pop top values `<= current`; none can be the current position’s strictly greater predecessor, and the newer current value dominates them for later queries.
After those removals, the top—if any—is greater and is the nearest surviving index to the left.
Write that top index, or the declared no-answer value when the stack is empty.
Push current only after answering, so current becomes a candidate for later positions and cannot answer its own previous-value query.

blocks.text: Previous-left queries read a survivor; they do not finalize popped entries as next-right scans do. Reading before removal can return a non-greater value, writing answers for popped entries changes the output owner, and pushing before the read makes current appear to precede itself. Reusable rule: identify whose answer is being written—current item or popped candidate—before ordering a monotonic transition.

items.prompt: In a left-to-right scan for each index’s nearest qualifying value to the right, the contract changes from strictly greater to greater-or-equal. Order the maintenance update for one current value.
constraints: Order the steps by semantic dependency, not by the order in which they are listed.
The canonical scoring contract awards preserved adjacent relations.

elements.text: Push the current item as unresolved after the frontier is restored.
Apply the new policy that equality is a qualifying relation.
While top value is less than or equal to current, pop that candidate and record current as its answer.
Stop when the stack is empty or its top is strictly greater than current.

feedback.reason: Changing the answer relation to greater-or-equal changes the resolving predicate from `<` to `<=`, so equal candidates are finalized by the current item.

items: State the new contract: equality now qualifies, so current resolves an earlier candidate when `candidateValue <= currentValue`.
For each qualifying top, pop its index and immediately record current as that candidate’s nearest right answer.
Stop at a strictly greater top or an empty stack; the resolving suffix is complete.
Push current as a new unresolved candidate.

blocks.text: For values `[5, 5]`, strict next-greater leaves the first `5` unresolved, while greater-or-equal resolves it at the second `5`; retaining the old `<` predicate would therefore be wrong. Popping all candidates ignores the stop boundary, and pushing first prevents current from resolving older equals. Reusable rule: changing `>` to `>=` in the output contract moves equality into the pop predicate and can change duplicate provenance.

items.prompt: Scan left to right for each index’s nearest later strictly smaller value; equals do not qualify. An increasing unresolved stack receives a smaller current value. Order the transition.
constraints: Order the steps by semantic dependency, not by the order in which they are listed.
The canonical scoring contract awards preserved adjacent relations.

elements.text: State the strict next-smaller predicate: a candidate resolves only when `current < top`.
While the predicate holds, pop one top index and record current as that index’s nearest smaller boundary.
Stop at an empty stack or a top less than or equal to current.
Push the current value and index after all violating tops are removed.

feedback.reason: Current must resolve and record every larger top candidate before it is pushed; stopping at `top <= current` restores the increasing frontier.

items: Use the strict contract to test `current < top`; equality must not resolve a candidate.
While true, pop one candidate and preserve its index long enough to write current as its nearest right smaller boundary.
Stop when the stack is empty or `top <= current`; that survivor is not resolved by current.
Push current after the frontier is restored.

blocks.text: For frontier values `[2, 5, 7]` and current `4`, current resolves `7` and `5` but not `2`, leaving `[2, 4]`. Popping all entries loses unresolved `2`; recording only after discarding indices loses answer ownership; pushing `4` first hides `7` and `5`. Reusable rule: a resolving loop must combine pop with answer recording, then stop at the first survivor that fails the exact relation.

items.prompt: For nearest strictly greater distance to the right, a left-to-right decreasing stack holds unresolved entries `[(9,0), (7,1), (4,2), (3,3)]` from bottom to top. Current `(10,4)` resolves several candidates. Order the transition.
constraints: Order the steps by semantic dependency, not by the order in which they are listed.
The canonical scoring contract awards preserved adjacent relations.

elements.text: Push the current value and index as unresolved.
Compare the current value with the top unresolved candidate.
Pop one smaller top candidate while the strict greater relation holds.
Write currentIndex - candidateIndex for that popped candidate.
Repeat pop and write for the remaining smaller suffix.

feedback.reason: Each smaller top must be popped and assigned distance `4 - candidateIndex` before the loop advances; current is pushed only after the full smaller suffix is resolved.

items: Compare current value `10` with the top unresolved candidate.
Because `10 > 3`, pop `(3,3)` while retaining its index.
Write distance `4 - 3 = 1` for that popped candidate.
Repeat for `(4,2)`, `(7,1)`, and `(9,0)`, writing distances `2`, `3`, and `4`.
After the smaller suffix is gone, push `(10,4)` as unresolved.

blocks.text: Every popped entry owns a distinct output, so recording only the final top loses two answers. Writing before popping lacks the candidate index, and pushing current first makes it block access to the entries it resolves. Reusable rule: in a next-right scan, one current item may finalize many candidates, but each pop and output write is one atomic logical step.

items.prompt: Compare two left-to-right tasks: (A) for every earlier index, write its nearest strictly greater index to the right; (B) for current index, write its nearest strictly greater index to the left. When is each answer obtained?
constraints: Use the exact output, strictness, scan direction, and tie semantics stated in the prompt.
Do not classify the algorithm from a variable name or one intermediate snapshot.

options.text: Both tasks write an answer only for the current index after current is pushed.
Both tasks write answers only after the entire scan, because no stack result is final during traversal.
Both tasks first push current, then use it as either its own left answer or its own right answer.
Task A writes for each popped earlier candidate; task B removes non-greater tops and writes the surviving top for current.

feedback.reason: The output owner differs: next-right finalizes popped earlier indices, whereas previous-left answers current from the nearest surviving top.

blocks.text: In task A, an earlier index remains unresolved until current is its first strictly greater value; the earlier index is popped and receives current immediately. In task B, current asks about the left side: remove tops that are not strictly greater, then the surviving top is current’s nearest qualifying predecessor. Waiting until the end loses nearest-event timing, while pushing current first lets an index answer its own query. Reusable rule: derive answer timing by naming the output owner—popped candidate for next-right, current item for previous-left.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.target_false_heuristic: Task A writes outputs owned by older popped indices, but task B writes the current index’s output from a surviving older index; one timing rule cannot describe both.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.surface_feature_classifier: Nearest answers become final during the scan. Deferring them is unnecessary and can discard which current item first qualified.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.unjustified_alternative_rule: Current cannot be strictly to its own left or right. Pushing it before querying creates an invalid self-candidate.

items.prompt: A next-strictly-greater-index scan reaches the end with unresolved candidates. Select all terminal strategies that are correct when their stated no-answer representation is the declared API contract.
constraints: Select all and only the statements that remain valid under the exact output and tie policy.
Each selected statement must be justified by retained-state semantics or a correctness/cost argument.

options.text: If the API uses `-1`, drain the remaining indices and write `-1` for each.
If outputs were initialized to `-1`, leave unresolved indices at `-1` without fabricating a resolver.
If the API declares `null` as no answer, write or retain `null` for each unresolved index.
Pop every remaining entry and fabricate the last input value as its answer.
Discard the remaining candidates silently because an empty stack is the required terminal state.

feedback.reason: End-of-scan candidates have proved absence of a qualifying value, so each must retain or receive exactly the API’s declared no-answer representation.

blocks.text: An index remains on the stack precisely because no later strictly greater value was encountered. At end of input that pending fact becomes a final absence result. A `-1` API may either preinitialize outputs and leave them unchanged or explicitly drain and write `-1`; a nullable API may use `null`. Fabricating the last input value creates a false qualifying answer, while silently discarding candidates without an already-initialized or explicit result leaves their outputs undefined. Reusable rule: terminal cleanup finalizes absence according to the output contract; it does not manufacture a comparison event.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.false_claim_1: The last input was already scanned and need not be greater than a remaining candidate; assigning it fabricates a resolver that never occurred.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.false_claim_2: Storage cleanup is not an output value. Unless outputs were already initialized to the declared absence marker, silent discard leaves results missing.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_1: Explicitly draining and writing `-1` finalizes every still-pending output under a `-1` contract.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_2: Preinitialized `-1` values already represent absence, so unresolved entries need no fabricated answer.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_3: A declared nullable result can preserve absence directly, but only because `null` is part of that API contract.

items.prompt: For every index, return the nearest previous index with a strictly greater value. While scanning left to right, the surviving top and current value are both `7`. Which duplicate rule is correct?
constraints: Use the exact output, strictness, scan direction, and tie semantics stated in the prompt.
Do not classify the algorithm from a variable name or one intermediate snapshot.

options.text: Push the current entry before checking the top, then repair any broken state afterward without changing the resulting answers.
Pop the older `7`: it cannot answer current, and current `7` is a nearer equivalent candidate for every future index.
Keep the older `7` and treat it as strictly greater than current.
Pop until the stack is empty; the stopping relation and answer timing are implementation details that cannot affect correctness.

feedback.reason: Under previous-strictly-greater index semantics, an equal top cannot answer current and is dominated by the newer equal index for all future positions.

blocks.text: The answer must be strictly greater, so the older `7` is invalid for the current `7`. For a future value below `7`, both equal candidates qualify, but the newer current index is closer; for a future value at least `7`, neither older nor newer `7` is strictly greater. Therefore the older equal is never preferable and may be popped by the `top <= current` rule. Keeping it can return a farther duplicate, treating equality as greater violates strictness, and popping unrelated larger tops would lose valid answers. Reusable rule: duplicate removal is safe only after checking both qualification and requested provenance such as nearest index.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.target_false_heuristic: Equality is not strict greater, and retaining the older equal can make a later query return a farther index than the newer equivalent candidate.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.surface_feature_classifier: A larger surviving top may still be the nearest strictly greater answer; emptying the stack discards valid provenance.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.unjustified_alternative_rule: Pushing current before removing the older equal leaves the dominated duplicate below it and skips the required answer query for current.

items.prompt: For nearest previous strictly greater index, the current position is the first element or all non-greater candidates have just been popped. The API uses `-1` for no answer. What does an empty stack mean?
constraints: Use the exact output, strictness, scan direction, and tie semantics stated in the prompt.
Do not classify the algorithm from a variable name or one intermediate snapshot.

options.text: No earlier strictly greater candidate exists for current, so write `-1` before pushing current.
Create a virtual earlier index `0` and return it as the previous greater candidate.
Pop until the stack is empty; the stopping relation and answer timing are implementation details that cannot affect correctness.
Push the current entry before checking the top, then repair any broken state afterward without changing the resulting answers.

feedback.reason: After all non-greater candidates are removed, emptiness proves there is no previous strictly greater index, so current receives the declared `-1`.

blocks.text: The stack contains exactly the earlier indices that remain possible strictly greater predecessors after dominance removals. If it is empty, no real earlier candidate satisfies the query, both for the first element and after a full pop. Therefore write the API’s absence marker `-1`, then push current for future positions. A virtual index is not an input candidate and may be returned as a fake answer; reading top without the empty check is invalid; pushing current first would make it appear previous to itself. Reusable rule: interpret an empty frontier through the output contract before mutating it.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.target_false_heuristic: The virtual index is not an earlier input whose value is strictly greater; returning it fabricates both provenance and qualification.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.surface_feature_classifier: Empty storage already means no answer. Treating cleanup as the goal omits the required `-1` result and ignores when current must be pushed.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.unjustified_alternative_rule: After pushing current, the top is current itself, which cannot be a previous index; the absence result must be written first.

items.prompt: For a left-to-right next-strictly-greater scan with a decreasing candidate stack, select all correct boundary observations.
constraints: Select all and only the statements that remain valid under the exact output and tie policy.
Each selected statement must be justified by retained-state semantics or a correctness/cost argument.

options.text: A singleton requires a special comparison rule that differs from the general contract.
Both monotone input directions necessarily empty the stack after every element.
A singleton remains unresolved and receives the declared no-answer result.
A strictly increasing input repeatedly resolves recent candidates and may keep the frontier small.
A strictly decreasing input performs no resolving pops and may grow the frontier to n entries.

feedback.reason: The single strict predicate `current > top` explains all three cases: singleton absence, repeated resolution on increasing input, and no pops on decreasing input.

blocks.text: In a left-to-right next-strictly-greater scan, pop while `current > top`. A singleton is pushed and never popped, so it receives the declared no-answer result. On `[1,2,3]`, each new value resolves the previous top and the frontier stays near one entry. On `[3,2,1]`, no current value is greater than its top, so all three indices remain and space reaches `n`. These are consequences of one rule, not special cases. The false singleton claim invents a second comparison, while the claim that both monotone directions empty the stack contradicts the decreasing trace. Reusable boundary check: run the exact predicate on singleton, monotone increasing, monotone decreasing, and duplicates.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.false_claim_1: A singleton simply never encounters a later resolver; the general strict predicate already yields the no-answer result.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.false_claim_2: On strictly decreasing input, every current value is smaller than the top, so `current > top` is never true and the stack grows.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_1: With no later element, the singleton cannot be popped by a qualifying current value and correctly remains unanswered.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_2: Each larger current value in a strictly increasing input resolves the recent smaller top, limiting the live frontier.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_3: No resolving comparison succeeds on strictly decreasing input, so all `n` unresolved indices may coexist.

items.prompt: For next strictly greater to the right, the decreasing unresolved frontier from bottom to top is `[9, 7, 4]`, and current value is `6`. Select all statements that describe the correct partial pop loop.
constraints: Select all and only the statements that remain valid under the exact output and tie policy.
Each selected statement must be justified by retained-state semantics or a correctness/cost argument.

options.text: Pop exactly one entry per input so the loop shape stays constant.
Pop only while the exact declared relation says the top candidate is resolved or invalidated.
Stop as soon as the surviving top satisfies the maintained invariant.
Allow older candidates below the restored frontier to remain unresolved for later input.
Continue popping until the storage is empty because more removal is always safer.

feedback.reason: Current `6` resolves top `4` but not `7`; the loop must pop by the exact relation, stop at the first survivor, and retain older unresolved candidates.

blocks.text: The predicate is `current > top`. With `[9,7,4]` and current `6`, pop `4` and record `6` as its nearest greater value. The new top `7` fails the predicate, so stop and then push `6`, producing `[9,7,6]`. Values `7` and `9` remain unresolved because `6` is not greater than them. Popping exactly one happens to work here but fails when current resolves several entries; popping to empty would falsely discard `7` and `9`. Reusable rule: loop cardinality is data-dependent, while the stopping condition is contract-dependent.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.false_claim_1: After `4` is removed, top `7` is not resolved by `6`; continuing to empty would delete two still-valid candidates.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.false_claim_2: Some current values resolve zero or many candidates. A fixed one-pop rule fails, for example, when current `10` resolves all three entries.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_1: The exact strict relation resolves `4` because `6 > 4` and rejects `7` because `6 > 7` is false.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_2: Stopping at `7` is precisely what restores the decreasing frontier before current is pushed.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_3: Older `9` and `7` have no qualifying current answer and must remain available for a later larger value.

items.prompt: In a next-strictly-greater scan, the unresolved stack contains older value `10`, and the newer current value is `6`. Select all statements that correctly reject removing `10` solely because `6` is newer.
constraints: Select all and only the statements that remain valid under the exact output and tie policy.
Each selected statement must be justified by retained-state semantics or a correctness/cost argument.

options.text: Recency determines scan order, not whether the older candidate is still valid.
For next-greater search, an older larger candidate can survive a smaller current value.
Removal must follow the exact comparison and output finality rule, not age alone.
Every older entry becomes obsolete when any newer entry arrives.
A monotonic stack is a FIFO queue in which newer entries always replace older entries.

feedback.reason: Newness establishes rightward position, but only the qualifying relation and output finality can remove an older candidate; `6` does not resolve `10`.

blocks.text: For next strictly greater, older `10` may be popped only by a later value greater than `10`. Current `6` is newer but smaller, so it cannot answer `10`; both values may remain unresolved. Recency tells us `6` lies to the right and can become a candidate, but it does not prove dominance. Replacing every older entry would lose `10` before a later `12` arrives, and calling the structure FIFO reverses the actual top-removal discipline. Reusable rule: encounter order is necessary for nearestness, but deletion additionally requires the exact comparison and a proof that the removed candidate’s output is final or dominated.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.false_claim_1: Current `6` is not greater than older `10`, so the older candidate remains unresolved rather than obsolete.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.false_claim_2: A monotonic stack removes from its top under a comparison predicate; it is not FIFO, and newer entries do not automatically replace older ones.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_1: Recency proves relative position only; it does not prove that `6` qualifies as greater than `10`.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_2: The concrete `10` then `6` trace shows an older larger candidate surviving a smaller current value.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_3: The strict comparison fails, so `10` has neither been answered nor shown irrelevant and cannot be removed.

items.prompt: A left-to-right scan originally returns each index’s nearest later strictly greater index by popping while `current > top`. The contract changes to nearest later greater-or-equal index. Which update is required for duplicates?
constraints: Use the exact output, strictness, scan direction, and tie semantics stated in the prompt.
Do not classify the algorithm from a variable name or one intermediate snapshot.

options.text: Pop while `current >= top`; an equal current value now qualifies and is the nearest such index encountered.
Keep `current > top`; equality affects only display text, not which index answers.
Pop until the stack is empty; the stopping relation and answer timing are implementation details that cannot affect correctness.
Push the current entry before checking the top, then repair any broken state afterward without changing the resulting answers.

feedback.reason: Because equality now qualifies, the resolving predicate must include it: `current >= top` finalizes an older equal at the nearest encountered index.

blocks.text: Under the old strict contract, `[5,5]` leaves the first `5` unresolved because `5 > 5` is false. Under greater-or-equal, the second `5` is a valid answer and, being the first qualifying value scanned to the right, is necessarily nearest. Therefore the pop predicate changes to `current >= top`. Keeping `>` misses valid equal answers, popping to empty can remove larger unresolved values, and pushing current first blocks it from resolving the older equal. Reusable rule: every change in strictness must be propagated through qualification, pop predicate, duplicate retention, and answer provenance.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.target_false_heuristic: With `[5,5]`, retaining `>` leaves the first index unanswered even though the second equal value now satisfies the contract.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.surface_feature_classifier: A top larger than current still lacks a qualifying answer; emptying the stack would remove it without justification.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.unjustified_alternative_rule: Once current is pushed, it hides the older equal candidate that it should resolve, so the relation must be applied first.

items.prompt: A routine for nearest strictly greater index to the right uses a candidate stack. A new task asks only whether the array contains any value greater than a fixed threshold `T`. A teammate proposes transferring the same per-index pop rule unchanged. Which response is correct?
constraints: Use the exact output, strictness, scan direction, and tie semantics stated in the prompt.
Do not classify the algorithm from a variable name or one intermediate snapshot.

options.text: Use the same per-index pop rule because every query mentioning “greater” has the same output contract.
Build and empty a candidate stack even though the task has no per-index nearest outputs.
Return true whenever any stack pop occurs; return false if the stack never pops.
The fixed-threshold existence task needs only a scan for any `value > T`; it has no pending per-index nearest answers that justify the old pop rule.

feedback.reason: The new output is one global boolean against `T`, so a direct scan is sufficient and the per-index nearest-candidate pop invariant no longer matches the task.

blocks.text: Nearest-greater-to-right produces one answer per index. Its stack retains unresolved indices, and the first later greater value finalizes each popped index. The threshold task instead asks one boolean: scan until some `value > T`, then return true; if none appears, return false. No index waits for a nearest resolver. A pop event is not equivalent to exceeding `T`—for `[1,2]` with `T=10`, a next-greater stack pops `1` but the correct boolean is false. Reusable rule: a shared comparison word does not transfer an invariant; re-derive state from output cardinality, provenance, and finalization timing.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.target_false_heuristic: The old rule tracks one pending nearest answer per index, while the new task asks one threshold boolean; the state and finalization obligations differ.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.surface_feature_classifier: A stack adds state without serving the boolean contract. Direct comparison with `T` is sufficient and clearer.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.unjustified_alternative_rule: A pop only proves current is greater than a previous stack value, not that current exceeds fixed threshold `T`; `[1,2]`, `T=10` is a counterexample.

contrastSets.transferBoundary: Transfer when strictness, scan direction, equality policy, or output timing changes; re-derive the exact pop predicate, answer timing, and terminal handling.
